Messages.Author: Henrik Klippstr?m
Messages.Body:
First - Border Skirmish? Anyone done something with this? Besides
wondering and decorating walls?

Second, I惴 sad to say I totally ignore the whole Anarch-concept. It愀
just never worth it. Yeah, I扉e seen the TWD-Anarch-decks.

The playable non-reprint library cards in the Anarch-set was:
- Aranthebes, The Immortal (My friends says this guy is great, and I
somewhat agree. But somehow I never manage to find place for him in my
decks. Maybe it愀 to few weenie-decks in our enviroment.)

- Bleeding the Vine (This one found it愀 way into some nasty
combo-decks (turbo-Baron, Revolt-Golconda-master-decks and into some
speed-bleed decks. Ie, decks that did not need any help.)

- Blow Torch (Simply a non-unique Sengir Dagger. Well balanced card.)

- Brinksmanship (Made the Slaughterhouse-bingers playable. Or maybe
not. That concept still needs some work from LSJ, because it messes up
the table balance - one player not bleeding/voting/rushing at all
makes his prey a little to powerful poolwise.)

- Drum of Xipe Totec (A gift for mr Goratrix. Well, how sweet.)

- Fiendish Tongue (Works good in Tzimisce. Actually, it gave birth to
a whole new type of Tzimisce-decks around here. Decks which I think
are much more funny then the old Wall-Smiling Jack-ish/Eagle Sight-ish
ones.)

- Filchware's Pawn Shop (Interesting card. A while it made us not
play equipment-based decks at all.)

- Gather (Best card in the set? Maybe. Maybe not. Bringing out plenty
of large-cap gangrels low on blood is... doubtful. Only seen one
strong deck doing it.)

- Gift of Experience (Solid card. The advanced-concept needed this.
Could have been a action-card?)

- Life in the City (Works OK.)

- Magazine (Naaaah... I don愒 know. Looks good on the paper, but
haven愒 seen it make any real difference.)

- Reins of Power (Complicated for a dumbass like me, but I扉e noticed
it is very powerful. It ousts people.)

- Repo Man (Yeah, mostly fun, but also, I think, quite playable.)

- Sunset Strip, Hollywood (Solid card.)

- Year of Fortune (Good card. Kinda like Rumours, but even more easy
to make deals with. Everybody wants +1 hand size.)

I primarily see playing Bleeding with Suddens, otherwise it's unpredictable
whether you stop what you put Bleeding in to stop.

>- Blow Torch (Simply a non-unique Sengir Dagger. Well balanced card.)

I almost never play with Sengir either.

>- Brinksmanship (Made the Slaughterhouse-bingers playable. Or maybe
>not. That concept still needs some work from LSJ, because it messes up
>the table balance - one player not bleeding/voting/rushing at all
>makes his prey a little to powerful poolwise.)

Problem with this archetype is that: there's not enough testing of it; there
might never be enough testing because it's so unpleasant.

>- Drum of Xipe Totec (A gift for mr Goratrix. Well, how sweet.)
>
>- Fiendish Tongue (Works good in Tzimisce. Actually, it gave birth to
>a whole new type of Tzimisce-decks around here. Decks which I think
>are much more funny then the old Wall-Smiling Jack-ish/Eagle Sight-ish
>ones.)

I wish this hadn't been made as I see it pretty much only helping Tzimisce
block decks. Tzimisce bleed decks were fine with Computer Hacking.

>- Filchware's Pawn Shop (Interesting card. A while it made us not
>play equipment-based decks at all.)

Why!, why does anyone think this card is any good? How often can you rely on
people to have: Equipment? Equipment in their ash heap? Equipment you gain
want to be playing in their ash heap? Do you really want to spend extra pool
to make sure it does anything?

Then, it could have been a Life in the City, a power non-trifle master, or a
non-master.

>- Gather (Best card in the set? Maybe. Maybe not. Bringing out plenty
>of large-cap gangrels low on blood is... doubtful. Only seen one
>strong deck doing it.)

Supposedly, this has been useful in at least one deck I can recall being
posted. I can't see playing it. It's unreliable in nature even ignoring that
it can be burnt before it can be used.

>- Gift of Experience (Solid card. The advanced-concept needed this.
>Could have been a action-card?)

Many times, I've gone to build mergy decks. Most times, the effort never
results in a deck as there's so little to be had by trying to merge. Of those
efforts that produced decks, I believe I once put in Gift. Likely was a
mistake. You could just play Effective Management instead which is a vastly
better card even if it doesn't guarantee merging.

>- Life in the City (Works OK.)
>
>- Magazine (Naaaah... I don愒 know. Looks good on the paper, but
>haven愒 seen it make any real difference.)

Coaster.

>- Reins of Power (Complicated for a dumbass like me, but I扉e noticed
>it is very powerful. It ousts people.)
>
>- Repo Man (Yeah, mostly fun, but also, I think, quite playable.)
>
>- Sunset Strip, Hollywood (Solid card.)
>
>- Year of Fortune (Good card. Kinda like Rumours, but even more easy
>to make deals with. Everybody wants +1 hand size.)

This is another card whose use boggles my mind. In a number of decklists I've
seen, the deck could have run Rumors instead which has an awesome effect once
it's in play where this has an ass effect once it's in play. Alternatively, it
could be all sorts of other high quality vote cards.

From my first pass of trying to rate all of the cards (though I didn't rate all
as some I wanted to look at more), the good to better than good library,
non-reprints:
The Anarch Free Press*
Anarch Railroad*
Aranthebes
Bleeding the Vine
Drum of Xipe Totec
Fee Stake: (all)
Fiendish Tongue
Firebrand
Gambit Accepted
Life in the City

* Cards I'd consider taking off the list.

Cards I'd put on the list:
Repo Man
Sunset Strip

Cards I still don't feel comfortable rating:
Nosferatu Bestial
Unlicensed Taxicab

Comment about the vampires: How many Anarch vampires do you see commonly
played in actual games? Sure, I see a lot of decklists for advanced Tegyrius
(and others like Nadima) and hear about nearby groups that try to merge him.
But, the only ones I see played by my regular opponents on a basis more often
than hardly never are Michael Luther, Christopher Houghton, Lucita, and Velya.
And, Smallpox, but I discount that as it's due to one deck that gets played a
lot and only played to pull off the combos rather than because it does anything
productive.

strike-type CEL cards anyway, right?

Messages.Author: John Flournoy
Messages.Body:
"Kevin M." <you...@imaspammer.org> wrote in message news:<XzJPb.33737$Xq2.26985@fed1read07>...

> > - Drum of Xipe Totec (A gift for mr Goratrix. Well, how sweet.)

>
> Why anyone would waste a Goratrix action equipping this drum when Infernal
> Pact exists is beyond me. I mean, you are going to be playing multiple
> strike-type CEL cards anyway, right?

Many, many, many players did not have access to an Infernal Pact (much
less several) before the reprint in Black Hand. It's still much easier
to pack a combo of Drums and Magic of the Smiths in quantity than it
is to pack the same number of Infernal Pacts, and the MotS's can be
used to find other equipment. I'd much rather have 2 Drums and 3
MotS's in a Goratrix/CEL deck than 5 Infernal Pacts. And most players
don't have 5 Pacts to begin with.

Plus, the Drum provides more than the Pact can; the Pact does not also
give a free maneuver each combat (which is huge when you're planning
to use Goratrix's theft-for-2 as your main strike.

Also, people sometimes play with both - give Goratrix the Drum, and
then pass it to someone else once their (often only) copy of the Pact
comes up.

> Kevin M., Prince of Henderson, NV (USA)

-John Flournoy

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>> Problem with this archetype is that: there's not enough testing of
>> it; there might never be enough testing because it's so unpleasant.
>
>I know someone that has made two players cry with this HoS deck, and yet he
>continues to play it constantly. I love hearing that. >:)
>
>What makes you think that the playtesters don't playtest these cards enough?

I don't recall mentioning playtesters. As an alternate win condition
archetype, I would normally expect every play group to have at least one
Brinksmanship deck. That doesn't seem to be the case. So, in trying to
determine the cause of the paucity of such decks, I fall back on my own reasons
for avoiding testing Brinksmanship decks, which involves not being all that
enthralled with spending a lot of time annoying people while trying to tune a
deck that may never be any good.

Now, if we want to take this in another direction, I'm sure V:TES playtesters
don't test the cards enough. Just as I'm sure playtesters of most CCGs don't
test the cards enough. Just as I'm sure that designers/product
managers/whatever sometimes ignore or undermine playtester efforts. Why am I
sure of these things? Because I've done a lot of CCG playtesting, have even
done V:TES playtesting. Then, I could just look at the product put out. The
only CCG I think *might* have proper playtesting, not that I know because I've
never worked with WotC, is Magic.

As a different way to win, every play group in existence should have looked at
the viability of it in order for proper testing to have been done. While one
member of my regular group played around with it for a while, I don't consider
that sufficient testing as he never discussed with anyone how to make the deck
competitive nor did he take his deck and test under tournament conditions
before giving up on it. Similar lacking of proper testing as far as I can tell
in the case of a player I mostly only see at tournaments who has played milling
in tournament play as I've never heard him discuss how to turn his deck into a
winning deck.

I'm not entirely sure what is meant by the line above about decks that don't
see tournament play. Obviously, lots of decks don't get played in tournaments.
I played four constructed tournaments last year which means I played around 4%
of the decks I built last year under tournament conditions. But, if a deck is
ever to compete with known decks, then I'd think it would have to be tested
under tournament conditions at some point. OTOH, a single tournament isn't
likely to generate suitable testing either as deck building is apparently one
of the least important factors to winning.

> I'll bite, what cards show evidence of hasty playtest and design in
> this game? How would more playtesting by a small group of people have
> shown that? Sometimes it takes a community to break a card.

Liberty Club Intrigue, Mistrust, Trainer, Bear-Baiting, Delivery Truck,
Magazine, for starters.

In my opinion, longer and better playtesting is more important for
making cards *strong enough* rather than not brokenly overpowered. It's
relatively easy (not to say that it's automatic, there are indeed a lot
of possible card combinations and not every group will see the important
ones) to identify and get depowered things that are over-strong.
(Though there is then a risk of them getting depowered so much that they
end up too weak in reaction.) Cards that start out too weak (or too
narrow, a form of weakness that I have particular trouble with) need
more playtesting to get them upgraded to a playable level, I think.

Obviously production deadlines have an impact on this and it's not
possible to playtest indefinitely. But more playtesting is almost
always better. It's always seemed kind of strange to me that VTES
playtesting isn't open (Shadowfist playtesting was, when I was involved
in it), both in the sense of "open to anyone who wants to test" and
"open between playtest groups who can communicate with each other". I
found that the players being able to bounce ideas off each other was
very productive in terms of brainstorming ways to break things and ways
to improve things that aren't good enough. It was also helpful that a
number of the Shadowfist designers participated in the open discussions.
Of course, not everyone's style is the same, which could be why VTES
doesn't operate like this. (I also have the sense that White Wolf feels
more strongly that if all their players were also playtesters, they
wouldn't sell as much product; I have no idea whether that's true or
not.)

Josh
